name: Freya Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What does a usual workday involve for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage six people who write and update product training for a large medical-device company. I check whether a new guide matches the approved instructions, find someone to answer field staff’s questions and chase overdue translations. I was promoted eight months ago and still need my oldest trainer to catch unclear explanations. I enjoy when a technician can use a guide on a real visit; I dislike sending a glossy page that hides a missing safety step.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like, and how much room do you have if your job changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband, Arjun, runs a small electrical contracting business; our children are eight and sixteen, and we have a mortgage. I have a bachelor’s degree, high pay for this role and about eight months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other corporate training offices nearby, though most write the same kinds of guides. I use AI now and then for a first outline after the technical team approves a source, but I wait for colleagues to prove a tool before using it in a live guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team to keep the approved instructions beside every draft. A faster outline does not help a technician if the safety step is missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be comfortable staying in training while I improve as a manager. Eight months saved and Arjun’s electrical work give us room for an ordinary gap, though the mortgage is always due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep our Friday check with the oldest trainer and compare any AI outline with the approved safety steps before publication. In the first year Arjun and I would continue a 200 monthly mortgage overpayment only while his customer invoices are paid on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. The job still asks us to explain real equipment accurately, and we can pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the last safety step nearly lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A draft left out the waiting time before opening a powered panel. The trainer caught it, and I held the guide until an engineer confirmed the wording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tie the mortgage payment to his invoices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband’s customers sometimes pay late. I would not send extra money to the lender while my husband’s electrical business needs cash for wages.

A missing **safety step** matters more than a faster outline.
think: My **training role** stays useful in a plateau.
Our **eight-month reserve** and Arjun’s work cover an ordinary interruption.
do: Check each **AI outline** against approved safety instructions.
Overpay the **mortgage by 200** only if Arjun’s invoices arrive on time and crew payroll remains covered.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household bills.
S0.quote: I would not send extra money to the lender while my husband’s electrical business needs cash for wages.
fieldNote: She uses AI **sometimes**, after source approval and colleague proof.
Eight months saved buffer the household, but **invoice timing** matters.
The older trainer catches **safety omissions** she still misses.

steps.text: Keep Friday guide checks and compare AI outlines against approved safety steps
Overpay mortgage by 200 monthly only if invoices arrive on time and crew wages stay covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI will write first guides and answer routine technician questions, so we must test it on actual repairs. I’d tell management which safety errors it makes before cutting a trainer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our six-person writing team could be cut in half, and I am the newest manager. I know the equipment story better than the software, but that may not save a job built around drafting and checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d compare the tool’s answers with forty logged field questions, marking every unsafe instruction. In the first year I’d learn the audit screen from our oldest trainer on paid time and ask the technical director for a posted field-support vacancy only if its written wage stays near mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about being displaced, but I want the error list in my hands. A smaller writing team could leave one manager, and it might not be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would see the unsafe answers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The engineers who sign the instructions and the trainers who take technician calls. If the tool says open a live panel, the finding must not sit in my private notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paid support job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after Arjun and I compare the written wage with our mortgage and business costs. I won’t take a field-support job if its written wage leaves our mortgage unpaid.

say: I’d test **field questions** before cutting trainers.
Management should see **unsafe answers** alongside staffing plans.
Engineers should approve the **safety source** behind every answer.
think: A smaller team could remove **my new manager post**.
Drafting and checking remain **exposed tasks** even if I know the equipment.
do: Test **forty logged questions** for unsafe answers.
Learn the **audit screen** on paid time and seek posted field support at viable pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller team.
S1.quote: I won’t take a field-support job if its written wage leaves our mortgage unpaid.
fieldNote: She tests **unsafe instructions** rather than writing speed.
Her new-manager status makes a **team cut** personal.
Field support requires **posted work** and written pay covering family costs.

steps.text: Compare AI answers against forty logged technician questions
Learn the audit screen from the trainer during paid work time
Apply for posted field support only if written wages cover mortgage and business costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for a named engineer on every safety instruction and written terms for trainers whose roles end. I’d tell technicians not to trust an unsigned answer from a new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could write, check and answer as well as I can, so I expect my training post to disappear. Arjun’s hands-on electrical work may last until robots arrive around 2031, but his invoices vary and one business cannot safely carry every family bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Arjun and I would postpone the planned house extension and keep the deposit in cash. Before 2028 I’d ask whether his business has enough paid installation work for an apprentice and complete electrical safety training only if we can pay its fee without touching payroll; after AGI arrives, I’d join an installation crew only with a written wage that covers our mortgage share and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. Eight months saved lets us talk rather than run, but it does not turn me into a safe electrician in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you just help with his invoices instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could do the quoting and scheduling by 2028, so I would not call Arjun’s office work a safe fallback. I would need supervised hands-on hours and a proper wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if his business cannot afford a trainee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep searching for posted paid trainee places at other firms. I will not take money from my husband Arjun’s crew wages to invent a place for me.

say: I’d insist on a **named safety signer** for each instruction.
Trainers need **written job terms** before their roles close.
think: Arjun’s physical work may last until **2031 robots**, but his invoices vary.
do: Postpone the **house extension** and keep its deposit available.
Check **paid trainee work** and safety training only if crew payroll stays protected.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing my wage.
S2.quote: I will not take money from my husband Arjun’s crew wages to invent a place for me.
fieldNote: She does not treat the family firm’s **office tasks** as safe from AGI.
A crew role depends on **paid work** and protected payroll.
She knows **2031 robots** also threaten electrical installation.

steps.text: Postpone the house extension and hold its deposit in cash
Complete electrical safety training only if its fee does not reduce crew payroll
Ask Arjun whether his business has enough paid installation work for a trainee
Join an installation crew after 2028 only with written pay covering mortgage share and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets people earn an apprenticeship place before the training office changes. I’d ask electrical firms for real wage figures rather than promises about skills shortages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn safe installation under a licensed electrician before AGI reaches my desk in 2031. Arjun’s quotes and my job’s writing would still face that thinking system; physical installations then face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d apply for a paid electrical apprenticeship at Arjun’s firm only if his accounts show a funded place without cutting current crew wages. I’d arrange school pickup with him before accepting shifts, and if he cannot fund it I’d apply to advertised places at other firms only when their wages cover our mortgage; in the first year after AGI, I’d continue only while paid supervised installations remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but I can check the accounts and the work before leaving my salary. Five years gives our younger child time to get used to a different pickup routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would sign off the work you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A licensed electrician, not Arjun just because he is my husband. I would not put my name on an installation I cannot safely inspect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the only other place pays much less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current salary while it lasts and keep looking. The mortgage has no family discount.

Five years lets people finish **paid training** before office work changes.
think: My desk work and Arjun’s quotes face **2031 AGI**.
Physical installations face **2034 robots** after that.
I could learn **licensed installation** before AGI reaches my desk.
do: Apply for a **funded family-firm place** only without cutting crew wages.

Continue **installation work** after 2031 only while paid supervised jobs remain.

S3.quote: The mortgage has no family discount.
fieldNote: Her family-firm plan needs **funded accounts** for a real place.

She keeps **childcare and wage gates** before any shift change.

steps.text: Apply for a paid family-firm apprenticeship only if accounts fund it without crew wage cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade lets families pay down debt and ask firms to offer apprenticeships with published wages. I would not tell young staff that writing training guides is a lifetime job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, with our older child grown and the younger one finishing school. I could reduce the mortgage and learn installation slowly, but the training guide work and Arjun’s quoting still face 2036 thinking AI. Robots reach physical electrical work around 2039, so the apprenticeship is a route with an end date too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Arjun and I would put an extra 250 monthly against the mortgage only when his crew payroll and our emergency reserve are covered. I’d take paid supervised installation days over the next two years only if his firm has real customer jobs, and seek a written installer offer before 2036 only if it covers the mortgage; after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while human installation work is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, with room to plan. A decade gives us time to see whether the business can support another worker without putting the house behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow against the house to expand the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would rather keep the business the size its paid jobs support than make the family mortgage answer for an empty work van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say look at paid apprenticeships as well as degrees, and ask what a real employer pays. I would not pick their path for them.

do: Pay **250 extra monthly** only after crew wages and reserves are covered.

fieldNote: She refuses to **risk the house** on business expansion without demand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my training team could vanish before I can work safely on an installation, and Arjun’s quotes would be exposed too. A paid supervised place backed by actual jobs, written wages and time for school pickup would help. Family business is only support if it can pay its workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs a safety step when software writes the whole guide. A technician still needs someone willing to put a name beside the danger.

headlineQuote: A technician still needs someone willing to put a name beside the danger.
portrait: **Freya**, 43, is a new training-content manager with a bachelor’s degree.
High pay and **eight months saved** support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses AI **occasionally**, after source approval and colleague testing.
She considers **paid electrical installation** only if the family firm protects crew wages and childcare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her training role before she can safely join an installation crew.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid supervised place**, actual customer work, written wages and school-pickup time would help.
